record.original_question: A positive integer is called a pseudo-prime of third kind if some nontrivial permutation of its decimal digits is prime. Among those numbers, are there infinitely many that are themselves prime?

evidence.quote: Question: How many pseudo-primes of third kind are prime numbers? (We conjecture: an infinity).

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Call a positive integer $n$ a "pseudo-prime of the third kind" if its decimal representation admits at least one nontrivial permutation of its digits (i.e., a permutation other than the identity, yielding a number possibly with the same numerical value but obtained by a non-identity rearrangement of digit positions) such that the resulting integer is prime. 

Question: Are there infinitely many positive integers $n$ that are themselves prime and are also pseudo-primes of the third kind? Equivalently, do there exist infinitely many primes $p$ whose decimal digits can be nontrivially permuted to produce a prime?
artifact.status_search_result: The question is posed as a conjecture (with the expectation that the answer is yes, there are infinitely many). No proof or disproof appears in the literature; standard references on permutable/digit-permutation primes do not resolve this weaker variant. The status appears to remain open.

status_evidence.title: Permutable prime - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: Article discusses primes that remain prime under all digit permutations; no infinitude result for the weaker 'some nontrivial permutation' version is stated.
status_evidence.claim: Related literature on digit-permutation primes does not resolve the existence of infinitely many primes admitting some nontrivial digit-permutation that is prime.

status_evidence.title: UNM Digital Repository document on pseudo-primes
status_evidence.snippet: Conjectures that there are infinitely many pseudo-primes of the third kind that are prime.
status_evidence.claim: The question is posed as an open conjecture.
